blocks.content: OAuth 2.0 is the standard that lets one application access your data in another application without ever seeing your password. When you click "Continue with Google" or let a photo app read your Google Drive, OAuth is the protocol working behind the scenes.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396521156-126287840.png

The core promise of OAuth is delegated access. You give a third party limited permission to act on your behalf, you decide exactly how much it can do, and you can take that permission back at any time. This page explains what OAuth is, the roles involved, the main flows, and how to reason about it in a system design interview.
1. The Problem OAuth Solves

Imagine a printing service that wants to print the photos stored in your cloud account. The naive solution is to hand the printing service your cloud username and password so it can log in and download your photos. This is a bad idea for many reasons.

["The printing service now knows your password and could do anything your account allows, not just read photos.","If you want to revoke access, your only option is to change your password, which breaks every other service too.","You cannot limit the service to read only, or to just one album. It has full control.","If the printing service is breached, your password leaks along with it."]
items: The printing service now knows your password and could do anything your account allows, not just read photos.
If you want to revoke access, your only option is to change your password, which breaks every other service too.
You cannot limit the service to read only, or to just one album. It has full control.
If the printing service is breached, your password leaks along with it.

blocks.content: OAuth was designed to remove passwords from this picture entirely. Instead of sharing a password, you grant a scoped, revocable token that represents a narrow slice of access.

blocks.title: The one line summary
blocks.content: OAuth lets an application get limited access to your account on another service, without you ever giving that application your password.
2. Authorization, Not Authentication

This distinction trips up many engineers, so it is worth stating clearly. OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework. It answers the question "is this application allowed to access this resource on the user behalf". It does not, by itself, tell an application who the user is.

People often use OAuth to log in ("Continue with Google"), but logging in is really an identity question. That layer is provided by OpenID Connect, which sits on top of OAuth and adds an identity token. We cover that split later on this page.

{"headers":["Concern","Question it answers","Handled by"],"rows":[["Authentication","Who is this user","OpenID Connect (on top of OAuth)"],["Authorization","What is this app allowed to do","OAuth 2.0"]]}
OAuth on its own proves permission, not identity. Treat a raw OAuth access token as a key, not as proof of who is holding it.
3. The Four Roles
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277762097-322716813.png
Every OAuth interaction is a conversation between four parties. Naming them precisely makes every flow easier to follow.

["Resource Owner: the user who owns the data and can grant access to it. This is usually you.","Client: the application that wants access, such as the printing service or a mobile app.","Authorization Server: the service that authenticates the user and issues tokens, for example Google accounts or an identity provider.","Resource Server: the API that holds the protected data and accepts access tokens, for example the Google Drive API."]
items: Resource Owner: the user who owns the data and can grant access to it. This is usually you.
Client: the application that wants access, such as the printing service or a mobile app.
Authorization Server: the service that authenticates the user and issues tokens, for example Google accounts or an identity provider.
Resource Server: the API that holds the protected data and accepts access tokens, for example the Google Drive API.

blocks.content: In many products the authorization server and the resource server are run by the same company, but they are logically separate responsibilities. The authorization server issues tokens; the resource server trusts and validates them.
4. Access Tokens and Scopes
The output of any OAuth flow is an access token. The client sends this token with every API request, usually in an Authorization header, and the resource server checks it before returning data.

GET /v1/photos
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJI...token...
blocks.code:
GET /v1/photos
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJI...token...

codes.http:
GET /v1/photos
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJI...token...

blocks.content: What the token looks like

An access token can be opaque, meaning it is just a random string the resource server looks up, or it can be a JWT that carries claims the resource server can validate on its own. Opaque tokens are easy to revoke because the server checks them against a store on every call. Self contained JWTs scale better because no lookup is needed, but they are harder to revoke before they expire.
Scopes

A scope is a string that limits what the token can do. When the client asks for access, it lists the scopes it wants, and the authorization server shows those to the user on the consent screen. The user is agreeing to exactly those scopes and nothing more.

["A photo printer might request only photos.read, so it can view images but never delete them.","A calendar assistant might request calendar.events.write to create meetings.","A backup tool might request broad read access across several resource types."]
items: A photo printer might request only photos.read, so it can view images but never delete them.
A calendar assistant might request calendar.events.write to create meetings.
A backup tool might request broad read access across several resource types.

blocks.title: Least privilege
blocks.content: Always request the narrowest scopes your feature needs. Over asking scares users at the consent screen and increases the blast radius if your token leaks.
5. The Authorization Code Flow
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277763735-391930330.png

This is the flow you should reach for by default, and the one interviewers expect you to know. It is used by web apps and, with an added protection called PKCE, by mobile and single page apps. The key idea is that the sensitive token exchange happens on a back channel that the browser never sees.

["The client redirects the user to the authorization server with its client id, the requested scopes, and a redirect URI.","The user authenticates and approves the requested scopes on the consent screen.","The authorization server redirects the user back to the client with a short lived authorization code.","The client sends that code, along with its client secret, directly to the authorization server from its backend.","The authorization server verifies everything and returns an access token, and usually a refresh token.","The client calls the resource server with the access token to fetch the user data."]
items: The client redirects the user to the authorization server with its client id, the requested scopes, and a redirect URI.
The user authenticates and approves the requested scopes on the consent screen.
The authorization server redirects the user back to the client with a short lived authorization code.
The client sends that code, along with its client secret, directly to the authorization server from its backend.
The authorization server verifies everything and returns an access token, and usually a refresh token.
The client calls the resource server with the access token to fetch the user data.

blocks.content: The clever part is step three and four. The browser only ever sees a temporary code, not the real token. The code alone is useless without the client secret, which lives safely on the server. This is why the flow is resistant to token theft through the browser.
The redirect URI matters

The redirect URI is where the authorization server sends the user back after consent. The authorization server must match it exactly against a pre registered list. If it did not, an attacker could ask for a code to be delivered to their own site. This single check prevents a whole class of code interception attacks.
6. A Concrete Walkthrough

Let us trace the photo printer example end to end, so the abstract roles become concrete. The printer is the client, you are the resource owner, your cloud provider runs both the authorization server and the resource server.

["You click \"Import from Cloud\" in the printer app, which redirects you to the cloud provider login with the scope photos.read.","You log in at the cloud provider, which is a site you already trust, and see a consent screen saying the printer wants to view your photos.","You approve, and the cloud provider redirects you back to the printer with a short lived authorization code.","The printer backend exchanges that code plus its client secret for an access token.","The printer calls the photo API with the token and downloads only the images you allowed."]
items: You click "Import from Cloud" in the printer app, which redirects you to the cloud provider login with the scope photos.read.
You log in at the cloud provider, which is a site you already trust, and see a consent screen saying the printer wants to view your photos.
You approve, and the cloud provider redirects you back to the printer with a short lived authorization code.
The printer backend exchanges that code plus its client secret for an access token.
The printer calls the photo API with the token and downloads only the images you allowed.

blocks.content: At no point did the printer see your password, and you can revoke its access later from your cloud account settings without changing anything else. That is the entire value of OAuth in one story.
7. PKCE and Why It Exists
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396521156-649040805.png

Mobile apps and single page apps cannot keep a client secret private, because anyone can decompile the app or read the JavaScript. Without a secret, a stolen authorization code could be exchanged for a token by an attacker. PKCE, which stands for Proof Key for Code Exchange, closes this gap.

["Before starting, the client generates a random secret called the code verifier and hashes it into a code challenge.","It sends only the code challenge when requesting the authorization code.","When exchanging the code for a token, it must present the original code verifier.","The authorization server hashes the verifier and checks it matches the earlier challenge."]
items: Before starting, the client generates a random secret called the code verifier and hashes it into a code challenge.
It sends only the code challenge when requesting the authorization code.
When exchanging the code for a token, it must present the original code verifier.
The authorization server hashes the verifier and checks it matches the earlier challenge.

blocks.content: An attacker who steals the authorization code still cannot use it, because they do not have the matching code verifier. PKCE is now recommended for every client type, not just public ones.

blocks.title: Modern default
blocks.content: For any new mobile or browser based client, use the authorization code flow with PKCE. The older implicit flow is discouraged.
8. Client Credentials Flow
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277767382-947416250.png
blocks.alt: Machine to machine client credentials flow

blocks.content: Not every OAuth interaction involves a human. When one backend service needs to call another with no user present, it uses the client credentials flow. Here the application is the resource owner acting on its own behalf.

POST /oauth/token
grant_type=client_credentials
client_id=service-a
client_secret=...
scope=reports.read

The service sends its own id and secret and receives an access token representing itself. There is no browser, no consent screen, and no user. This is the right choice for machine to machine communication such as a nightly job pulling data from an internal API.

Because there is no human to revoke access through a consent screen, you protect these tokens by keeping their scopes tight, rotating the client secret regularly, and issuing short lifetimes so a leaked secret has limited value.
9. Other Grant Types
OAuth defines several grant types for different situations. Knowing when each applies, and which are now discouraged, shows maturity in an interview.

{"headers":["Grant type","Use case","Status"],"rows":[["Authorization Code","Web, mobile, and SPA user login","Recommended, with PKCE"],["Client Credentials","Machine to machine, no user","Recommended"],["Device Code","TVs and devices with no browser or keyboard","Recommended for its niche"],["Implicit","Old browser apps returning tokens directly","Discouraged, replaced by code plus PKCE"],["Resource Owner Password","App collects the user password directly","Strongly discouraged"]]}

The password grant defeats the whole point of OAuth by making the client handle the password, so avoid it except for trusted first party legacy cases. The implicit flow exposed tokens in the URL and is now replaced by the authorization code flow with PKCE.
10. Refresh Tokens

Access tokens are deliberately short lived, often lasting minutes to an hour, so that a leaked token expires quickly. A refresh token is a longer lived credential used to obtain new access tokens without asking the user to log in again.

POST /oauth/token
grant_type=refresh_token
refresh_token=...
client_id=...
client_secret=...

["Store refresh tokens securely, ideally on the server or in secure device storage, never in plain browser storage.","Support rotation, where each use of a refresh token issues a new one and invalidates the old one.","Allow revocation so a user or admin can cut off a compromised session immediately."]
items: Store refresh tokens securely, ideally on the server or in secure device storage, never in plain browser storage.
Support rotation, where each use of a refresh token issues a new one and invalidates the old one.
Allow revocation so a user or admin can cut off a compromised session immediately.

blocks.title: Rotation catches theft
blocks.content: With refresh token rotation, if both the attacker and the real user try to use the same refresh token, the server detects the reuse and can revoke the whole chain.
Choosing token lifetimes

There is a tradeoff in how long tokens live. Short access tokens limit the damage of a leak but force more refreshes; long ones are convenient but dangerous if stolen. A common balance is access tokens measured in minutes and refresh tokens measured in days or weeks, paired with rotation and the ability to revoke.
11. OAuth vs OpenID Connect
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396521157-609536422.png
blocks.alt: OAuth access token vs OIDC ID token

blocks.content: OpenID Connect, usually shortened to OIDC, is a thin identity layer built on top of OAuth 2.0. It reuses the same flows but adds one important thing: an ID token.

["The access token is for calling APIs. It says what the client may do.","The ID token is a JWT that describes who the user is, including fields such as name, email, and a stable user id.","OIDC also defines a standard userinfo endpoint and a discovery document so clients can integrate consistently."]
items: The access token is for calling APIs. It says what the client may do.
The ID token is a JWT that describes who the user is, including fields such as name, email, and a stable user id.
OIDC also defines a standard userinfo endpoint and a discovery document so clients can integrate consistently.

blocks.content: If your goal is "let users log in with Google", you actually want OIDC, not raw OAuth. If your goal is "let this app read a user calendar", plain OAuth with the right scopes is enough. Many providers give you both at once.
Why people confuse the two

Because both start with the same redirect and consent screen, they look identical from the outside. The difference is what you do with the result. If you read the ID token to establish who the user is, you are doing authentication with OIDC. If you only use the access token to call an API, you are doing authorization with OAuth. Using an access token to identify a user is a classic and dangerous mistake.
12. Common Security Mistakes
OAuth is secure when implemented carefully, but several mistakes appear again and again in real systems.

["Not validating the redirect URI strictly, which lets an attacker steal the authorization code by redirecting it to their own site.","Skipping the state parameter, which is needed to prevent cross site request forgery on the callback.","Treating an access token as proof of identity instead of using an ID token for that purpose.","Requesting far more scopes than the feature needs.","Storing tokens in insecure places such as local storage that is exposed to cross site scripting.","Forgetting to verify the token signature and expiry on the resource server."]
items: Not validating the redirect URI strictly, which lets an attacker steal the authorization code by redirecting it to their own site.
Skipping the state parameter, which is needed to prevent cross site request forgery on the callback.
Treating an access token as proof of identity instead of using an ID token for that purpose.
Requesting far more scopes than the feature needs.
Storing tokens in insecure places such as local storage that is exposed to cross site scripting.
Forgetting to verify the token signature and expiry on the resource server.

blocks.title: The state parameter
blocks.content: Always send a random state value on the authorization request and check it matches on the callback. This ties the response to the request you actually started.
13. When to Use OAuth
OAuth is the right tool when access crosses a trust boundary, or when you want to delegate limited access rather than share full credentials.

{"headers":["Pros","Cons"],"rows":[["Third party apps need access to user data without the password","A simple single application with its own users and sessions may not need it"],["You want scoped, revocable permissions","It adds redirects, token management, and an extra server to run or integrate"],["You need social login or a single provider across many apps","Misconfiguration can create real security holes, so it needs care"],["Machine to machine access between services with client credentials",""]]}

For a small internal tool with one login system, plain session or token authentication may be simpler. OAuth earns its complexity when there are multiple parties or when delegation is the whole point.
14. In a System Design Interview
When a design touches third party login, delegated access, or API access for external developers, mention OAuth and be ready to defend the choices.

["Name the four roles for the specific system you are designing.","Default to the authorization code flow with PKCE for user facing clients.","Use client credentials for service to service calls.","Explain short lived access tokens plus refresh tokens with rotation.","Call out OIDC explicitly if the requirement is user login rather than API access."]
items: Name the four roles for the specific system you are designing.
Default to the authorization code flow with PKCE for user facing clients.
Use client credentials for service to service calls.
Explain short lived access tokens plus refresh tokens with rotation.
Call out OIDC explicitly if the requirement is user login rather than API access.

blocks.content: A strong answer separates authentication from authorization out loud, then picks the flow that matches who the client is and whether a human is present.
15. Common Interview Questions
Is OAuth used for login or for access: OAuth itself is for authorization, meaning access. Login is layered on top through OpenID Connect, which adds an ID token that proves identity.
Why not just share the password: a password gives unlimited, non revocable access and leaks everything if the client is breached. A scoped token gives limited, revocable access that expires.
What does PKCE protect against: it stops a stolen authorization code from being exchanged for a token by an attacker, which matters for clients that cannot keep a secret.
Access token vs refresh token: the access token is short lived and sent to APIs on every call; the refresh token is long lived and used only to get new access tokens.
What is a scope: a string that limits what the token can do, shown to the user at consent and enforced by the resource server.
16. Key Takeaways

["OAuth 2.0 grants delegated, scoped, revocable access without sharing passwords.","It is about authorization; OpenID Connect adds authentication on top.","The four roles are resource owner, client, authorization server, and resource server.","Default to the authorization code flow with PKCE for anything a user touches.","Use client credentials for machine to machine access.","Keep access tokens short lived and pair them with rotating refresh tokens.","Validate redirect URIs and use the state parameter to stay safe."]
items: OAuth 2.0 grants delegated, scoped, revocable access without sharing passwords.
It is about authorization; OpenID Connect adds authentication on top.
The four roles are resource owner, client, authorization server, and resource server.
Default to the authorization code flow with PKCE for anything a user touches.
Use client credentials for machine to machine access.
Keep access tokens short lived and pair them with rotating refresh tokens.
Validate redirect URIs and use the state parameter to stay safe.
